items: Know Your Legal Rights: Identify which federal law applies to your situation before deciding how to respond to a potentially illegal question during your interview.
Know Your Legal Rights: Memorize the five protected categories under Title VII—race, color, religion, sex, and national origin—so you can recognize when questions target these areas.
Know Your Legal Rights: Understand that under the ADA, interviewers can only ask about your ability to perform specific job duties, not about the nature or severity of any disability you may have.
Know Your Legal Rights: Recognize that the ADEA protects workers 40 and older, which means questions about your graduation year or career length are potential violations of federal law.
Respond In the Moment: Use a deflection phrase like "I'd prefer to focus on my qualifications for this role" when an interviewer asks something that makes you uncomfortable.
Respond In the Moment: Pause before answering any question that feels wrong—taking even five seconds gives you time to decide whether the question crosses a legal line.

Respond In the Moment: Ask the interviewer how the question relates to the job requirements when you're unsure whether something is appropriate, which redirects the conversation without accusing them.
Respond In the Moment: Decline to answer if the question is clearly about a protected characteristic, even if it feels awkward—your legal right to refuse is firmly established.
Protect Yourself After: Write down the exact questions asked, the interviewer's exact words, and the overall context of the conversation while everything is still fresh in your memory.
Protect Yourself After: File a formal complaint with the EEOC within 180 days of the incident if you believe your rights were violated—timing is critical to preserving your case.
Protect Yourself After: Evaluate whether the rejection you received might be connected to your refusal to answer illegal questions by reviewing the timeline and any communications you received.
Protect Yourself After: Consult an employment attorney about potential legal remedies if you have strong evidence that discrimination occurred during your interview process.
